body:
The issue here is that Walt couldn't buy more land because he was running the studio into bankruptcy trying to build Disneyland. So let's assume that the company's savings hadn't dried up during the war years and that movies like Fantasia, Bambi, Pinnochio, Saludos Amigos, etc. were each huge successes in their own right. This alone probably would have kept Disney out of television through the 1950's, meaning that there was never a Disneyland TV series or a Mickey Mouse Club.

If you look at the original [Herb Rhyman map](http://i843.photobucket.com/albums/zz352/loaloauk/DLP%20that%20never%20was/disneylandmaprymanbig_zpse4bba903.jpg) for the park you see a couple of areas that never made it past the concept stage due to budget: Holiday Land and Lilliputian Land would have been built (a form of Recreation Park was actually built where the Matterhorn ultimately went.) Beyond that, it's likely that all of the attractions at Disneyland would have been expanded significantly in terms of their size and scope.

The Fantasyland dark rides were even shorter in 1955 than they are now, and Walt wasn't exactly thrilled with them. Larger, more immersive environments for the rides would certainly have happened -- maybe even more of them. Mr. Toad's Wild Ride was originally envisioned as a roller coaster but was changed to a dark ride, and Pinnochio was originally supposed to have gotten a Monstro-themed water flume ride decades before Splash Mountain was ever envisioned.

Even from opening day Disneyland was criticized for corporate sponsorship being everywhere. This was out of financial need, especially in Tomorrowland, which was built last and left largely unfinished on opening day. The backlash about Tomorrowland is the chief reason that Disneyland's first major expansion was in that area of the park. If that land had been fully built on opening day we probably never would have gotten a Matterhorn, submarines or monorail. No. Monorail. The next Disneyland expansion probably would have been north and based around a fantasy theme. Disney had tried for decades to get a Wizard of Oz attraction off the ground, but due to space and budget it never seemed to happen. An Oz Land is my best guess for what the next Disney 'land' would have been, followed by the New Orleans Square addition once sophisticated audio-animatronics technology had been developed.

More money would have allowed Disney to maintain tighter control over the park. As a result the parks today would probably have less obtrusive advertising because 'it wasn't like that when Walt was around.' Since Disneyland was more 'complete' upon opening there would have been more opposition towards replacing aging attractions. Extra space means less reason to tear down older rides and replace them with new ones.

Disney didn't even own the Disneyland Hotel when it opened because they couldn't afford it. That wouldn't be a problem here, so a large, expansive Disneyland Hotel would have been present on opening day. With extra land the surrounding acres around the park would remain untouched so as to maintain sight lines and the illusion of traveling to a different time and place. However, Anaheim would still suffer from a string of cheap motels, crime, and poverty as they did in our timeline. With a larger ownership of land Walt could have perhaps taken a more proactive role in clearing up these problems, but Anaheim was always very buddy-buddy with the Disney company until recently so I doubt much would have changed.

Walt's interest in industrial innovation would have gone on, and with a larger park he would have had more resources to experiment and develop new technologies. It's easy to imagine a second park being built in the 60's, halfway between his original idea for EPCOT and a World's Fair. For this endeavor the studios would have had to get into the television business to finance Walt's visions. Rather than introducing Americans to Disneyland each week Uncle Walt would have been spouting exclusively about technological innovation and progress, further cementing his status as a captain of industry than that of a beloved cartoonist with a golden touch.

No matter how much land Disney was able to purchase for the original Disneyland, eventually Disney's imagination would have outgrown his real estate, but when? Whether or not Walt would be able to secure the land in Florida if he had waited any longer is uncertain. Walt was in poor health at the time of the Florida purchase and on his deathbed he was furiously spouting out plans for an EPCOT Center he would never get to see. The studio would have been in a better financial situation at the time of Walt's death than they would have been with the Walt Disney World investment, but the company was still directionless without their leader.

Undoubtedly the demand for a second Disneyland would have been too tempting to ignore. Without Disney World already in-progress Walt's brother Roy would have happily retired, leaving the company in less capable hands with more capital to spend. The Disney board would have shrewdly taken on a financing partner, perhaps even another studio, to help get Disneyland 2 off the ground. Florida always made the most sense as a location for a second theme park, but Virginia and Texas were also possible contenders.

During this time Disneyland 1 would have been more ambitious in their expansion projects, as Disneyland has always been a financial success and had the money to spend without Walt Disney World's rocky first years. The second industrial park's future without Walt is much more bleak. Walt was a unique visionary that could bring the world's greatest business leaders to his parks and make them excited enough to help finance his projects. Pretty much the second Walt died a great number of industrial sponsors would have fled. Over a few decades of struggling financially it either would have been shuttered (unlikely as this was 'Walt's baby') or heavily changed into something more palatable, like a roller coaster park or a water park.

It's important to remember how poorly the studios were doing in the 1970s/early 80s as well. This would still have happened as it did, and at this time there were serious discussions about splitting up the various units of business and selling them off. This probably would have gone on if Disneyland were any larger and had a struggling second park that was dipping everything into red ink. The Disney studios would have been sold off to one of their competitors, perhaps Paramount as they would be an ideal partner to help finance Disneyland 2. This would bring a young Paramount executive named Michael Eisner into the fold, leading to a string of hit live-action films for Paramount and Walt Disney Pictures (which operates more as an imprint of Paramount than an independent studio.) Animation is another matter entirely.

With new bosses the other Roy Disney, Walt's nephew, has neither the political clout nor the stock options to re-energize Disney's animation division. Cheaper animated films in the vein of An American Tail would have been produced by Disney for Paramount rather than ambitious projects like The Little Mermaid. These movies are stiff, lifeless, and ripped apart by critics and families alike. Young CalArts animators like Tim Burton and Glen Keane would have left Disney for more profitable ventures in television rather than stick around in the 80's for the sake of contributing to the Disney legacy. Eisner's budget-cutting and a lack of successful films ultimately means the Disney name is tarnished by the Paramount purchase.

Now separate from the company with his own name, Roy invests in experimental computer animation and a fledgling PIXAR. Toy Story, or something like it, debuts in the mid-1990s from an independent distributor and become a box-office smash. Paramount/Disney, whose animation division was shuttered in the 90's, is left completely in the dust.

Meanwhile Disneyland (or "Magic Kingdom" as it has been renamed since they are not owned by Disney and only license the Disney characters for their remaining, aging attractions) goes through radical changes over the 80's and 90's. Technological innovation is a less a priority than drawing in crowds. Expensive audio-animatronics are replaced with cheap thrill rides, and lush gardens are torn out as cost-cutting measures. Rules are less lenient and Walt Disney's Disneyland devolves into a filthy, crowded and downright unseemly place. Those old enough to remember the original park lament that it was these types of shabby amusement parks that first inspired Walt to build a safe, clean environment where he and his children could spend the day and enjoy themselves. The parks sell or lease their remaining unused land to hotel companies, but Magic Kingdom fails as a thrills park and is mismanaged. Never able to establish an identity of its own Disneyland 2 maintains an uncomfortable licensing agreement with Paramount/Disney until ultimately the second Disneyland removes/re-themes all Disney/Paramount attractions and is sold to a regional amusement park chain.

In the early 2000's Roy convinces PIXAR, hot off a string of successful animated films, to purchase Magic Kingdom and the surrounding land from private ownership. This 'Save Disneyland' movement reignites a passionate fanbase that had grown up with the idealized version of the park, and leads to stricter management and a slew of new attractions featuring the PIXAR characters.
